articles.title: A Michigan woman bought wooded land beside Detroit's airport in 1997; after a fight over trees exceeding aviation height limits, a November 2026 appeals court upheld an injunction and rejected her compensation claims
articles.summary: While a patch of woods can offer privacy, natural beauty and a sense of isolation, property ownership near a major airport comes with restrictions that
articles.body: While a patch of woods can offer privacy, natural beauty and a sense of isolation, property ownership near a major airport comes with restrictions that can reach well above ground level. The height of trees on one Michigan homeowner’s property became the basis of a long legal battle against the authority that operates Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport. Nearly three decades after buying the land, she suffered a major blow to her court battle when an appellate decision allowed the airport authority to enforce aviation safety restrictions.A dispute over property with roots in aviation safetyAccording to the Michigan Court of Appeals, Michelle Baldwin bought a wooded property in 1997 on Vining Road, south of Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport. To the north was property owned by the Wayne County Airport Authority. The dispute began after the Joint Airport Zoning Commission for Wayne and Washtenaw Counties approved an airport zoning ordinance in July 2016. The rule established tree and structure height limitations within a 20-mile radius of the airport, and anything above the limits was considered a potential aviation hazard. Baldwin’s property was in Zone B, which meant that trees and other objects could only be up to 50 feet above the elevation of the airport.Warnings and disputes over cutting down treesThe Michigan Court of Appeals pointed out that some trees on Baldwin’s property eventually grew taller than the prescribed height. Airport contractors have conducted obstruction surveys around the airport in 2018, 2021 and 2022 to identify possible risks.An airport authority representative told Baldwin in February 2022 that eight trees on her property were too tall and posed an aviation hazard. The authority is understood to have offered to arrange for them to be removed but Baldwin refused the offer in May that year.The dispute also included allegations of unlawful entry. Baldwin alleged that airport authority employees had gone onto her property and cut down or trimmed between eight and 11 trees without permission between 2018 and 2022. The authority confirmed its employees had removed at least one tree, though its representative said the organization had been unaware of the entry at the time.Court denies compensation claimsThe airport authority filed suit in February 2023, seeking an injunction that would force Baldwin to remove or trim the trees or allow its representatives onto the property to correct the violations.Baldwin filed counter-claims, arguing that the restrictions constituted a regulatory taking of her property, and that the alleged tree removal entitled her to damages under Michigan's timber-trespass law.The trial court ruled for the airport authority, holding that the maintenance of trees in excess of aviation safety restrictions constituted a public nuisance. The bottom line: removing the hazards was not a compensable taking of private property.Appeals court upholds injunctionThe Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court’s decision in its November 3, 2026 ruling. A judges’ panel of a court of appeals ruled airport hazards were a public nuisance under state law and the authority had the authority to take steps to remedy the violation. They also denied Baldwin’s claim for compensation, finding the enforcement measures did not deprive her of the productive use of her multi-acre property.Her timber trespass claim was also dismissed as the acts of the authority were part of an authorized government function protected by government immunity.The court also made it clear that its decision did not give the airport authority free rein to cut down trees on private land The ruling supports the injunction and underlines the importance of aviation safety regulations for properties located near major airports.Images Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: 'Genocide against Italians': Over 6,000 Italy schools get bomb threats, similar warnings in UK & Ireland
articles.summary: More than 6000 schools across Italy received bomb threats and over 300 plus were evacuated on Wednesday after receiving identical bomb threat emails
articles.body: More than 6000 schools across Italy received bomb threats and over 300 plus were evacuated on Wednesday after receiving identical bomb threat emails warning of a “genocide against the Italians”, triggering security sweeps and disrupting classes across the country.The threats were sent to educational institutions in several regions, from Rome to Friuli in the north and Basilicata in the south. Students and staff were moved to safe areas while police searched school premises for explosives.The email was signed by a sender identifying himself as “Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan”, according to a government source familiar with the matter. It claimed that a powerful explosive device with a remote detonator had been placed inside a school building and threatened to kill Italians in a mass attack. The message also claimed that a bomb had been planted in the engine of prime minister Giorgia Meloni's car.Education minister Giuseppe Valditara told Italian broadcaster La7 that at least 300 schools had received the alerts, adding that the number could rise. A school in Rome informed parents that all students had been moved to safety and were being supervised by teaching staff.At a high school in Rome, students initially mistook the evacuation alarm for the recess bell and learnt about the threat only after leaving the building. “They are saying it was a bomb alert because an email arrived from Russian hackers in which they said they would have killed everyone. It was pretty violent,” 18-year-old student Anita Bartocci told AP reporters.Police are investigating the threats, a spokesperson for Rome police said.The latest incident comes less than 10 days after a similar barrage of threatening emails reached more than 270 Italian schools on November 2, including institutions in Rome. Those alerts also prompted evacuations and security checks, but turned out to be false.Similar threats reported abroadSchools in Ireland, Scotland and Northern Ireland also received threatening messages, although no evacuations were reported in those countries.Police in Northern Ireland said they were conducting “urgent inquiries” after an email was sent to hundreds of schools. Police Scotland said it was treating similar messages as hoaxes and had not advised schools to evacuate, adding that its assessment was that they did not represent a credible threat.Irish police said they were aware of a “generic communication” sent to several educational institutions.The pseudonym Mikhail Andropov has appeared in other threatening emails sent in recent days to European television broadcasters. The sender has also reportedly claimed responsibility for threats targeting flights, although authorities have not established whether the incidents were connected.The school alerts come amid a wider pattern of disruption in Europe, including false threats against aircraft and cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems. Recent attacks on cold-storage facilities have also affected blood banks in France, forcing staff to move blood supplies to alternative storage units.However, investigators have not established that the school threats, flight alerts and refrigeration attacks are connected or part of a coordinated campaign.Italian defence minister Guido Crosetto described the school threats as an attempt to spread fear and uncertainty. He said law enforcement agencies were working to distinguish genuine dangers from threats made by people seeking to cause disruption, warning that such incidents could become increasingly frequent.The interior ministry has also stepped up its response. Interior minister Matteo Piantedosi convened senior security officials on Tuesday to discuss the growing cyber threat. The meeting concluded that some attacks were aimed not simply at disrupting systems but at spreading unfounded alarm, destabilising institutions and damaging their credibility.Former interior minister Marco Minniti called for a dedicated intelligence capability focused on cyber security, arguing that the threat required cooperation across political lines and should be treated as a matter of national security.You use AI every day. articles.title: The election is over: It's time for young Jews to step up and lead
articles.summary: The election may be over, but young Jews still face a defining choice: Let antisemitism shape their future or build strong Jewish communities and become the leaders they want to see.
articles.body: A week has passed since Election Day. The votes have been counted. But no election can decide how proudly we live as Jews, how we support one another or what kind of leaders we become. Those decisions belong to us. As the former student body president at the University of California, Santa Barbara, I know what it means to lead while your Jewish identity becomes a target. My experience, featured in the documentary "October 8," taught me how urgently institutions need to confront antisemitism — and how much courage it can take to speak up when they fail. It also taught me that we cannot put our lives or our leadership on hold until someone else finds that courage. JEWISH TEENS PREPARE TO COMBAT ANTISEMITISM ON CAMPUS WITH HISTORY, HUMOR AND COURAGE Recently at the Jewish Student Union Presidents Conference in Stamford, Connecticut, I saw hundreds of Jewish high school students putting that principle into practice. They had gathered as the country headed into Election Day. But their leadership did not depend on who would win. They were already building Jewish communities in their schools. Already taking responsibility for something larger than themselves. Already choosing to show up. I recognized myself in them. I am a Jewish Student Union alumna. Before I became a student body president, I needed opportunities to understand my Jewish identity, develop my voice and discover that I had something worth contributing. BACK TO SCHOOL SHOULD NOT MEAN BACK TO FEAR FOR JEWISH STUDENTS Returning to speak with these students reminded me why that early investment matters. Leadership grows through practice: inviting someone to a first meeting, organizing a program, asking a difficult question or standing beside a classmate who feels alone. Those actions can seem small. For the person on the receiving end, they can change everything. Too often, we talk about young Jews only in terms of what is happening to them. The harassment they face. The friendships they lose. The pressure they feel to distance themselves from Israel or explain away a part of who they are. Those experiences deserve attention. Antisemitism must be exposed and confronted. But young Jews also deserve to be seen for what they are creating. CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS In Stamford, I saw students developing the skills and relationships that will shape their schools now and their college campuses later. They were learning to lead before a crisis demanded it of them. That preparation matters. A strong Jewish identity gives us something to draw on when others challenge our belonging. A community gives us people to turn to. The experience of speaking up once can help us do it again. We should be giving more young Jews those opportunities. We should also make room for the joy that makes Jewish life worth building in the first place. A student who encounters the Jewish community through music, sports or a celebration may discover a connection that a discussion about antisemitism could never provide. Those experiences give us friendships, memories and reasons to keep showing up for one another. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Last week’s Omer Adam concert at Barclays Center offered a powerful example: thousands of people gathering around Hebrew music, Jewish pride and a shared connection to Israel. Among those celebrating were wounded Israeli warriors. Their presence brought another dimension to that joy: the opportunity to stand alongside people who have sacrificed so much and welcome them into a shared celebration. That is why I want to thank Warriors of Israel, which supports Israel’s wounded warriors. Its work reminds us that building a Jewish community means taking responsibility for one another, including helping those living with the consequences of their service find support, connection and joy. For young Jewish leaders, there is a lesson in that kind of commitment. We can build communities that celebrate who we are while making sure people who need us feel included and supported. That spirit belongs in our schools and on our campuses, too. We need Jewish life that welcomes people in. We need students who know how to organize, build friendships across differences and explain what they believe. We need leaders who can confront hatred without allowing it to consume their entire sense of purpose. None of this releases elected officials or university administrators from their responsibilities. They must enforce rules against threats and harassment. They must confront antisemitism within their own political circles. Jewish students have every right to demand accountability from the institutions that serve them. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER And we can make those demands while taking responsibility for the communities we want to build. Run for student government. Start the club your school is missing. Invite the student who is hesitant to join. Learn enough about your history to speak about it with confidence — and enough about someone else’s experience to listen with care. You do not need a title to begin. You need a willingness to act and the humility to keep learning. The students I met in Stamford will enter a world full of challenges. They will also enter it with ideas, conviction and the ability to make a difference. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP My message to them, and to young Jews across this country, is simple: Become the leaders you want to see in the world, regardless of who holds political office.

articles.title: Fury v Joshua fight in Cardiff faces objections over 3am finish
articles.summary: The fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium is due to finish in the early hours to align with US primetime.
articles.body:
Concerns have been raised by residents over plans for next month's eagerly awaited Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua fight in Cardiff to run into the early hours of the morning.

The all-British heavyweight fight is due to take place at Principality Stadium on 11 December, with the event expected to finish at 03:00 GMT the following day to align with prime-time viewing in the United States.

But as part of the stadium's application to extend licensing hours , Cardiff Council has received objections related to concerns about anti-social behaviour, noise, traffic and public safety.

The council's licensing subcommittee will meet to discuss the proposals on 25 November.

The stadium operates a curfew until 01:00 when the roof is closed but has requested permission for licensed activities, including the sale of alcohol and the playing of music, to continue until 03:00 on 12 December, with the venue remaining open until 03:30.

The Principality Stadium is in Cardiff city centre, which is part of its attraction, but there are also residential properties nearby.

One person who lives directly opposite the stadium wrote to the council saying they supported the event taking place, but called for extra conditions to be put in place "to protect residents living immediately around the stadium".

"My representation relates to the prevention of public nuisance and the prevention of crime and disorder," the resident wrote.

The resident called for a dispersal plan for streets around the stadium, with stewards in place until crowds have cleared, no amplified music outside the stadium after midnight and for street-cleaning to be completed by 08:00 on 12 December.

Three others also wrote to the council, calling for the application to be rejected, with one arguing the "noise and late-night disturbance" would not come to an end when the event finishes.

"Music, amplified sound, large crowds, shouting, vehicles, taxis and people leaving the stadium can all result in disturbance continuing well into the early morning," the resident wrote.

Another resident with young children said the event running into the early hours of the morning would "cause absolute chaos for those of us living right next to it".

The person said issues such as "shouting and singing" early in the morning would "completely wake the whole house up and leave us with exhausted, stressed children".

Others wrote in support of the licensing conditions being granted, with one saying they believed the event would bring a "significant economic boost" to businesses in the city.

Another said the event could help bring more tourists, particularly from the United States, to Cardiff.

One of the most eagerly awaited bouts in recent boxing history, numerous venues were put forward when the fight was proposed, including New York's Madison Square Garden .

However, focus shifted to the UK after Joshua and his promoter Eddie Hearn refused to budge on their contractual right to stage the fight on British soil.

Wembley Stadium was touted as a potential venue - with London Mayor Sadiq Khan urging promoters to get in touch - but its strict 23:00 event curfew proved an issue given Netflix's preference to broadcast during prime time hours in the US.

In Cardiff, while early-hour finishes require extensive co-ordination around transport, policing and crowd management in the city centre, the venue already holds a precedent for late-night boxing.

In 2007, Joe Calzaghe's super-middleweight unification victory over Mikkel Kessler did not start until 02:00 local time to satisfy US television network Showtime.

The stadium's application for the variation of the licence has been made according to the Licensing Act 2003, with a 28-day consultation period allowed.

Representations can be made to object to or support the proposals around prevention of crime and disorder, public safety, public nuisance and protection of children from harm.

If objections are received, the council's licensing sub-committee must meet to hear them, and "may modify the conditions of the licence or reject the whole or part of the application".

The Principality Stadium has been asked to comment.

articles.title: Senior doctors call off two-day strike planned this month
articles.summary: Consultants in England were due to walk out on 25 November in disputes over pay and working conditions.
articles.body:
Consultant doctors in England have called off their two-day strike this month to hold talks with the government.

The walkout was due begin on 25 November at 06:59 GMT, with consultants staffing emergency care only.

This is known as Christmas Day cover and was likely to have a major impact on most routine and elective or planned services.

But the British Medical Association, the trade union for doctors, said it was pausing the action to discuss pay and working conditions with the government.

Consultants – the most senior doctors in hospitals – were given a 3.5% pay increase this year.

But the BMA argues pay has fallen by a quarter over the past 17 years, once inflation is taken into account – although this is using a measure of inflation that tends to be higher than the one favoured by economists.

The union also wants a reduction in the standard working week, from 40 to 35 hours, and higher pay for out-of-hours work, alongside changes to pensions, including greater flexibility over when they can be taken.

Meetings have been taking place over recent months, but the BMA is now entering formal talks with the government's negotiating team. They could start as soon as this week.

In a statement, BMA consultants committee co-chairs Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta said: "We welcome the opportunity to enter formal negotiations with the government and hope this marks a turning point in a dispute that has gone on for far too long.

"We've always said strikes do not need to go ahead as long as the government is willing to genuinely negotiate and now is their chance to do so.

"We have received assurances that there are no constraints on what we discuss in these negotiations, and we look forward to hearing their proposals on both pay and working conditions."

But government sources said giving them a bigger pay rise this year was not on the table because of the state of the public finances and current level of their pay.

Average earnings for consultants top £150,000 a year.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the cancellation of the strike was "welcome news for patients and the wider NHS".

"I had a constructive discussion with the BMA on reforms that could give consultants a stronger voice, greater flexibility and more freedom to innovate, while improving services for patients."

In the strike ballot, 76% of consultants who took part voted in favour of strike action, with just over half of eligible BMA members taking part.

The government says this represents only around one in five consultants employed by the NHS in England voting for strike action, as nearly half are not BMA members.

articles.title: US soldier arrested for Russia spying: What we know
articles.summary: A 41-year-old man has been arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under the National Security Act.
articles.body:
British police have arrested a senior member of the United States military on suspicion of spying for Russia following an investigation by counterterrorism officials, marking the latest instance of alleged espionage in the West linked to Moscow.

A 41-year-old man was arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under Section 1 and Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023, according to a statement by London Metropolitan Police.

Section 1 of the Act relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.

“As part of the investigation, officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire. The country to which the allegations relate is Russia,” the statement read.

So far, not much information is available about the soldier who was arrested.

The BBC reported on Tuesday that the soldier was based at the Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire.

Those barracks serve as the base for NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC), which is a strategic operational base for the military alliance.

The man has been detained under the National Security Act 2023, which allows police to hold him without charge for 14 days, the Metropolitan Police said, adding that Counter Terrorism Police London were leading the investigation.

Under British law, police generally do not publish the names of suspects before they have been charged, except in exceptional circumstances.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for Britain’s Counter Terrorism Policing, said the arrest and investigation resulted from “close collaboration between UK and US authorities”.

“The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing. This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved. We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security.”

The investigation into the US soldier is not connected to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations, according to the Metropolitan Police.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the arrest involved allegations of espionage which are of the “utmost concern” to the US and its allies.

“While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners,” Patel said.

He said that the FBI had made 167 arrests in counterintelligence and espionage-related cases over the last 21 months – a 53 percent increase over the comparable previous period.

Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, said the case demonstrated the strength of the UK-US partnership.

“I am grateful to the UK and the FBI for their professionalism and teamwork throughout this investigation. The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent. I encourage anyone who thinks they’ve witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office,” he said.

This is believed to be the first time a US soldier was found to be under suspicion of spying for a foreign government while in the UK.

However, espionage allegations have grown in recent months.

In October, British police arrested three men on suspicion of helping Russian intelligence under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023.

A month before, three people — two men and a woman — were arrested on suspicion of spying for Moscow.

The UK has been one of Ukraine’s biggest backers since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and relations between London and Moscow are at their lowest.

However, even before the Ukraine war, Russian intelligence had played a role in London. In 2006, former Russian spy Alexander Litvinenko was poisoned in the capital and in 2018, there was an attempted plot to poison double agent Sergei Skripal.

articles.title: African rights body raises alarm over treatment of Niger’s Mahamid Arabs
articles.summary: Rights commission appeals to Niger president over alleged abuses against Mahamid.
articles.body:
The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights has appealed to Niger’s president over alleged violations of the fundamental rights of the country’s Arab Mahamid community, amid reports of restrictions on access to water, education, healthcare and identity documents.

In an urgent appeal sent to President Abdourahamane Tchiani on November 6, three commission representatives raised concerns about the treatment of the community in the southeastern Diffa region. The appeal was made public on November 9.

The signatories included the commissioner responsible for the human rights situation in Niger and the heads of two working groups covering economic, social and cultural rights, and the rights of Indigenous populations, communities and minorities.

The Mahamid are an Arab community with historical links to Chad and Sudan. Many live in Niger’s Diffa region. Some families have been settled there for generations, following successive waves of migration from neighbouring countries.

Disputes over their nationality and identity documents have repeatedly put them at odds with the authorities.

What allegations have authorities made against the community?

Officials have accused some Mahamid residents of obtaining nationality documents fraudulently, trafficking arms and having links to armed groups around the Lake Chad basin.

At a security meeting in Diffa on August 22, Governor Mahamadou Ibrahim Bagadoma and other officials discussed nationality papers, cross-border movement and security, as well as tensions over water and grazing land, according to state news agency ANP.

ANP reported that Bagadoma warned against holding the entire Arab community responsible for allegations involving particular individuals. The accusations have not been independently verified.

What rights concerns has the African Commission raised?

The appeal comes amid reports of measures restricting the Mahamid’s access to basic services and official documents.

Nigerien publication African Perceptions said it had obtained a copy of an Interior Ministry radio message dated October 7 and numbered 002235, addressed to the governors of Diffa and Zinder.

According to the publication, the message instructed authorities to close schools and water facilities used by the Mahamid, require community members to pay the full cost of healthcare and stop issuing civil status documents to them. It also called for the withdrawal of existing documents, including national identity cards and passports, and for security forces to enforce the measures.

Al Jazeera has not independently authenticated the document or established whether the instructions have been implemented.

The commission has expressed concern about the reported restrictions on access to water, education and healthcare, as well as identity documents. Its appeal to President Tchiani is not a formal finding that the government has violated the community’s rights.

Could the community be forced to leave Niger?

Chadian broadcaster Radio Ndarason Internationale reported that Mahamid representatives were told at a meeting in Diffa on November 8 that they had two months to leave Niger.

The meeting was reportedly attended by the Diffa prefect, the Gueskerou administrator, the Komadougou canton chief and village chiefs. Radio Ndarason said the community representatives declined to comment when approached.

Nigerien publication La Roue de l’Histoire reported on November 10 that the authorities had set December 31, 2026, as the deadline for the community to leave.

Neither publication has made a formal expulsion order available. Al Jazeera has not independently confirmed the decision, its legal basis or whether it applies to the entire community.

Niger faced a similar dispute in 2006, when the government announced plans to expel Arabs from Diffa to Chad. The operation was suspended after protests and negotiations.

articles.title: Harry Styles was photographed carrying a small charity's tote bag; the publicity helped generate $40,000 in sales, and the project has since funded 1,300 therapy sessions for people struggling to pay for care
articles.summary: A single photo of pop star Harry Styles walking through London with a canvas tote bag has helped raise $40,000 for a small mental health initiative.
articles.body: A single photo of pop star Harry Styles walking through London with a canvas tote bag has helped raise $40,000 for a small mental health initiative. The money has paid for more than 1,300 therapy sessions for people who cannot afford treatment. The bag belonged to the Other People Fund, an independent project started by Elena Kilgore. What began as a small personal idea quickly grew into a major charity effort after the singer was seen carrying it.From a break-up line to a mental health missionThe idea started with a personal experience when Kilgore was 23. After a relationship ended and both people agreed to "see other people", Kilgore decided to seek therapy. However, she soon learned how expensive private treatment could be. This made her realise that cost was a major barrier for many people who needed mental health support. According to People, therapy sessions in the United States usually cost between $100 and $200. Knowing that many people cannot afford regular treatment, Kilgore decided to create clothing with a playful message: "I think that we should see other people, and by other people I mean therapists". In an interview with People, Kilgore explained that she first planned to keep the project small. She wanted to sell just 100 shirts and use the money to pay for therapy for a few people in her personal circle.A manifestation that reached LondonWhile creating the clothing line, Kilgore had Styles in mind as someone she hoped would support the project. "My five year plan for Other People Fund was to get Harry Styles in my t-shirt," Kilgore told Novel Magazine. "I designed it with him in mind. My exact direction to my shirt designer was, 'something that Harry Styles would wear.'" Kilgore contacted the singer's stylist through Instagram. The stylist bought both a shirt and a tote bag. A few weeks later, fans spotted Styles walking through London with the large canvas tote. Photos of the singer carrying the bag quickly spread across social media. This brought thousands of fans to the charity's website.Funding hundreds of mental health sessionsThe sudden attention had an immediate effect on sales. The brand made $40,000 directly from merchandise sales. The money went towards the project's non-profit organisation, Support for the Psyche. So far, the initiative has paid for 1,300 therapy sessions for people who need financial support. "It's so obviously cyclical that finance and mental illness are intertwined," Kilgore told Novel Magazine. She explained that although people are now more open about mental health, many still cannot afford the treatment they need. The project continues to sell merchandise, including special tote bag collaborations. All proceeds go directly towards helping people pay for mental healthcare.You use AI every day. articles.title: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax
articles.summary: More than 6,000 Italian schools received a threat. Authorities in all three countries say there appears to be no risk to the public. It is not known if the incidents are linked.
articles.body:
Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities.

In Italy a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution but Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger".

"These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook.

Scotland's education secretary Mairi McAllan said there was no risk to the public and specialist cyber-crime officers were working to identify the source of the messages. In Northern Ireland education officials told schools to remain open unless otherwise advised by police.

It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.

"As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," McAllan said.

Scottish police had earlier said that the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes. However some local authorities confirmed that some schools had been evacuated.

"Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails," Police Scotland said.

Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent on Wednesday to the inboxes of 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 state schools, and private schools were unaffected.

The message, said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan", caused alarm in many schools.

Italy's Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the incidents were probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk", adding that there appeared to be a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in across Europe targeting flights, supermarkets and even hospitals.

Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption.

Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.

No risk to public from hoax school bomb threats, says government minister

Police treating threatening email sent to more than 300 schools as 'hoax'

On Wednesday one Milan headteacher, Anna Bertato, told Italian media she had checked the email address of the sender online: "It was already classified as spam by a student at a university in Taiwan."

Another Milan headteacher, Massimo Nunzio Barrella, told Adnkronos news agency that he had immediately realised the email was spam when it arrived in his inbox at 08:59 and he decided not to evacuate his school and reassured parents who phoned in.

"The text seemed almost comical," said Barrella, "it was like a message from Martians: 'We have come to annihilate you.' I even had a bit of a laugh."

Although many schools were initially evacuated on Wednesday, the alarm was quickly lifted, and pupils were allowed to return to class. Some parents decided to take their children home for the day, but the majority of schools in Milan did not send their pupils home.

Some 280 school head teachers had already received threats in recent days, according to Italian reports.

In a statement, the head of the central Umbria region Stefania Proietti said "checks conducted so far in Umbrian schools have proved negative, and law enforcement is working rapidly and carefully to verify each report".

articles.body: Russia and Ukraine have agreed to carry out their biggest prisoner exchange since the start of their nearly five-year war, following two days of US-mediated negotiations in Abu Dhabi.The agreement emerged as the most significant outcome of the first direct meeting between the Russian and Ukrainian delegations in nine months. However, the discussions have yet to produce any major breakthrough on ending the war, with both sides continuing to hold firm on their demands.“One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalise the numbers tomorrow,” Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, said after the talks concluded.Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Ukraine's team, also confirmed the planned exchange.Russia and Ukraine have exchanged prisoners several times during the conflict, but expectations of a major diplomatic breakthrough were low ahead of the Abu Dhabi meeting.Kushner, Witkoff to meet Putin and ZelenskyyWashington is continuing its efforts to revive peace negotiations, which have so far failed to produce significant results.Kushner said he and US envoy Steve Witkoff would travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin. They would then fly to Dublin to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.The diplomatic push comes at a time when the Trump administration faces a changing political landscape. Democrats are set to take control of the US Congress in January following the midterm elections, potentially increasing pressure on Washington to provide greater support to Ukraine.Russia's wartime economy is also under considerable strain, while Ukraine continues to face devastating Russian attacks on its power infrastructure.Umerov said Ukraine's delegation was also expected to meet European officials on Wednesday.Although Moscow does not want European countries involved in direct negotiations, representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO were present in Abu Dhabi and held consultations with the Ukrainian delegation.Zelenskyy described Tuesday's discussions as “constructive and quite substantive”.He said the talks focused largely on humanitarian matters, including prisoner exchanges, the return of Ukrainian civilians held captive by Russia and children taken from Ukraine.Security guarantees for Ukraine were also discussed. However, neither Moscow nor Kyiv has indicated any willingness to compromise on its key demands.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the meeting as “very productive”, but cautioned that reaching an agreement to end the war would take time.Russia, Ukraine continue attacks despite talksThe diplomatic discussions took place against the backdrop of continued fighting along the front line, where neither side has made significant territorial gains this year.Both countries have also continued launching long-range missile and drone attacks.Overnight, Russian forces struck Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv, injuring seven civilians and damaging property.Russia's Defence Ministry claimed that its air defence systems shot down 627 Ukrainian drones overnight, including 150 over the region surrounding St Petersburg.Regional Governor Alexander Drozdenko said the drone attacks sparked a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, one of Russia's major oil export facilities. articles.title: Bradford Labour MPs jostle for £14.6 left by axed leisure centre plan
articles.summary: Over £14m is available to be spent due to the cancellation of a new leisure centre in Bradford.
articles.body:
Three Labour MPs in Bradford have found themselves scrapping it out for a share of £14.6m left over from a cancelled leisure centre project.

The Reform UK-led council axed the long-planned Squire Lane leisure centre project earlier this year, citing rising costs.

Shipley MP Anna Dixon had backed calls to use some of the money - which comes from a £20m government grant - to reopen Bingley Pool, while Bradford East MP Imran Hussain said last week he wanted a share to help turn a derelict building on his patch into a youth and community hub.

Meanwhile, Bradford West MP Naz Shah has recently said the cash should stay in the constituency it was meant for: "This money is something that I secured for Bradford West, and I'd like to keep it in Bradford West."

The competing calls for the funding follow a recent row over whether Bradford could keep the grant at all .

Council leader Stephen Place had initially disputed Dixon's claim that the money was available for other projects, but later confirmed that the government would not claw it back . He said at the time that the council was not yet able to commit it to a particular scheme.

Shah has now told the BBC that the council leader had "absolutely assured" her Bradford West would be given "priority" when the money was allocated.

But she also said it was ultimately a matter for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) to decide on.

The BBC understands the money has to be spent by 2028.

Asked whether the pot could be split between the three constituencies, hers and her two Labour colleagues', Shah pointed to the separate £20m allocated to Hussain's Bradford East constituency through the current government's Pride in Place programme.

She stressed it was every MP's own "choice and prerogative" to champion particular projects in their own constituencies with money earmarked specifically for those constituencies. "But the money that comes in to Bradford West, I'm very keen that it stays in Bradford West," she said.

Asked about her colleagues' efforts to secure some of the money , Shah said: "Is it the way I would have tried to get money for my constituency? No, it isn't."

But she said she had spoken to Dixon and understood why she was pressing for the swimming pool.

"That pool is something that she is passionate about, and rightfully so, because nobody would expect an MP not to be," Shah said.

Shah pointed to the Scotchman Road fields in Toller ward as one site on her patch that could benefit from investment and said there was further need across Bradford West, including in Clayton, Thornton, Manningham and Heaton.

"You could double and triple that [money], and I'd still find the need for it," she said.

Bradford Independents Group councillor Ishtiaq Ahmed, who is chair of the cross-party Bradford West Area Committee, also backed Shah's call, saying: "Bradford West must not lose the investment it was promised."

He said the original Levelling Up grant was intended to tackle deprivation and health inequalities , and urged the council to commit the full £14.6m to alternative projects in Bradford West if ministers agreed.

"The cancellation of the original Squire Lane project does not cancel the needs of the people it was intended to serve," he said.

"I have no objection to Bingley residents campaigning for their swimming pool. They are entitled to make their case. But why should Bradford West lose out?"

The Heaton and Frizinghall councillor said not investing the money in Bradford West would "represent a serious injustice".

The previous Conservative government had earmarked the £20m for the Squire Lane project through its Levelling Up programme.

But in July, the Reform-led executive decided to discontinue the project amid concerns about the council's financial position and rising costs. This was despite more than £5m of the original pot having already been spent on preparation and planning work.

The executive axed the project contrary to its own officers' recommendations, who had stressed in a report that the Bradford West area experiences "disproportionately high levels" of deprivation, physical inactivity, and poor physical and mental health.

Their report said Bradford West's lack of a publicly accessible swimming pool left "thousands of residents [facing] barriers in participating".

A Bradford Council spokesperson said the authority was "currently assessing options for alternative use of the Local Regeneration Funding previously allocated to the Squire Lane Leisure Centre project".

"Key to this is the need to ensure any projects are deliverable and can draw down on all required grant funds by end of March 2028," they added.

The BBC understands that a memorandum of understanding exists between Bradford Council and the MHCLG which sets out how Local Regeneration Funding is managed.

The authority would be expected to discuss any major changes with the MHCLG and while MPs would not have a formal role in that, they are considered to be significant stakeholders.

articles.title: Visitors to Guernsey from France more than double in three years
articles.summary: Figures from the States of Guernsey show "really encouraging" signs, Deputy Lee Van Katwyk says
articles.body:
The number of visitors to Guernsey from France has more than doubled since 2023, according to the latest figures.

Data from the States of Guernsey shows the number of people visiting the island from France between July, August and September in 2026 was up by 103%, compared with the same period three years ago.

The Guernsey Quarterly Travel and Visitor Accommodation Bulletin found the figure was up by 21% on this time last year, while visitors from the UK had also increased by 5% compared with the same period in 2025.

Deputy Lee van Katwyk, tourism lead for the committee for economic development, said the rise in visitors numbers was "really encouraging".

Van Katwyk said: "The increase in French visitors over the past few years is phenomenal, and something that we hope will continue to grow."

He also said "where these visitors are coming from is also really interesting" as the number of UK visitors increased.

Visitors from the rest of the world increased by 14% on last year and 38% on three years ago.

Data showed 119,664 visitors came to the island by plane, ferry or yacht during the third quarter of this year, an increase of 7% for the same period last year.

Day-trip and overnight visitor numbers also increased.

Co-chair of the tourism advisory board, Charlie Walker, said people were "more likely than ever to recommend the island to others".

"It's no surprise then that our number of returning visitors is up significantly," he added.

articles.title: Sneaky fee on airport purchase sparks outrage after traveler shares receipt: 'Out of control'
articles.summary: A traveler at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport found a 3% surcharge on a bookstore receipt, and the fee was taxed on top of it. A retail expert weighed in.
articles.body: A traveler is pushing back after discovering an unexpected fee on a bookstore receipt from a venue located inside New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport. The traveler, who posted on Reddit last week, shared a photo of a receipt from Bryant Park Market, a Hudson-operated store at JFK Airport's Terminal 5. The customer purchased "The Gales of November: The Untold Story of the Edmund Fitzgerald" by John U. Bacon for $21.99, only to discover there was an additional and unexpected charge on the receipt. PROBE UNDERWAY AS 7 FLIGHT ATTENDANTS SICKENED BY BAFFLING ODOR ON MAJOR AIRLINE "I just wanted to buy a book before my 6 a.m. flight," the user wrote. "And naturally, they tax on top of the added fee as well!" "A 3% surcharge has been applied to your purchase. This charge is for employee and retention programs and is not a gratuity," the receipt reads, as shown in the person's online post. It shows that 66 cents was added as part of a 3% surcharge, bringing the taxable subtotal to $22.65. The buyer then paid $2.01 in sales tax at the regular 8.875% rate, bringing the total to $24.66. The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey told Fox News Digital that the 3% Employee Benefits and Retention Surcharge was authorized in December 2024 and has been in effect for more than a year. HOW MUCH REST SHOULD FLIGHT ATTENDANTS GET? NEW PROPOSAL IGNITES FIGHT IN THE SKIES An official said the surcharge is designed to support annual wage increases for thousands of airport workers while helping retailers cover higher labor costs stemming from airport minimum wage requirements and the Healthy Terminals Act. Fox News Digital also reached out to Hudson, which referred questions to the Port Authority. Reddit users expressed frustration over the additional charge. "Hopefully they don't retain you as a future customer," one person wrote. "This hidden fee stuff is out of control," another said. "They need to change the laws, so things are marked [at] what they actually cost." CRUISE TIPPING CHARGES ARE 'OUT OF CONTROL,' SAY PASSENGERS AS COMPANIES TOUT 'EXCEPTIONAL SERVICE' A third user wrote, "I would have canceled the purchase when I saw it on the screen." Though the surcharge could be confused with a tip, Bryan Gildenberg, managing director of retail research and consulting firm Retail Cities, said it should not be considered a gratuity. "So I never really thought of it as a gratuity. And I don't know that that's the right way to think about it," Gildenberg told Fox News Digital. He added, "It's really more of a surcharge that the companies are allowed to charge to cover the cost of operating at the airport." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Gildenberg, based in Washington state, noted that operating a store at an airport is often more expensive than running one elsewhere, partly because employees face additional commuting challenges. "In any captive environment, the likelihood that you're getting great price value isn't very high." He said airport retailers try to keep their prices comparable to those outside airports despite higher operating costs. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Travelers should purchase necessities, Gildenberg said, before arriving at the airport whenever possible — and to expect to pay more if they don't have what they need. "The two best words to keep in mind [with] airport shopping are the Latin words caveat emptor, meaning let the buyer beware," Gildenberg said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ He described airport shoppers as a "captive audience." "Like in any captive environment, the likelihood that you're getting great price value isn't very high," he said. Gildenberg said the backlash is part of a broader picture involving consumer frustration with rising prices. articles.title: Trump touts legal victory over BBC as judge says his lawsuit against British broadcaster can proceed
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC will proceed after a judge rejected the outlet's motion to dismiss the case.
articles.body: President Donald Trump scored a victory in court Tuesday as a judge ruled that his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) can proceed. "A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth, just handed down by highly respected District Court Judge, Jeffrey T. Kuntz, of the Southern District of Florida," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Trump continued, "In his powerful ruling, Judge Kuntz wrote,'Here, the news entity created the story. BBC admitted as much by confirming it had edited a video to make it appear as though President Trump made a statement he never made.' We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!" JUDGE LIMITS BBC FROM RELITIGATING JAN 6 IN TRUMP LAWSUIT OVER MISLEADING DOCUMENTARY EDIT In his ruling, Kuntz criticized the BBC over how it edited the 2024 "Panorama" documentary at the center of the lawsuit, suggesting the broadcaster "knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement." "This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech. BBC also had the entire speech available to them for nearly three years by the time of the Documentary," the filing read. TRUMP WINS PERMISSION TO FILE AMENDED COMPLAINT IN $10B DEFAMATION LAWSUIT AGAINST BBC Kuntz did, however, dismiss Trump's second count in the lawsuit alleging the BBC documentary violated the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act (FDUTPA), finding that the documentary did not qualify as "commercial speech" under the law. The judge gave the BBC until Dec. 1 to respond to the remaining defamation claim. A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster was surprised by the ruling but respected the court's authority and remained confident in its legal position. "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process. It would be inappropriate to comment further while proceedings are ongoing," the BBC spokesperson told Fox News Digital. TRUMP THREATENED BY JUDGE WITH SANCTIONS IF HE DOESN’T SIT FOR DEPOSITION IN $10 BILLION BBC DEFAMATION SUIT Trump filed a $10 billion lawsuit against the BBC late last year for its 2024 "Panorama" documentary that distorted his remarks to supporters on Jan. 6, 2021. Critics claim the documentary was misleading because it omitted Trump's call for supporters to protest peacefully, splicing together separate portions of a lengthy address to give a wrong impression. "We're going to walk down to the Capitol. And I'll be there with you. And we fight — we fight like hell," the documentary showed Trump saying. In reality, Trump said, "We're going to walk down to the Capitol. And we're going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women, and we're probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them, because you'll never take back our country with weakness. You have to show strength, and you have to be strong." It wasn't until 54 minutes later that Trump called on his supporters to "fight like hell" for election integrity. The BBC previously apologized for the misleading edit and said it had removed the program from its platforms. Despite the apology, the broadcaster has maintained that the edit does not constitute defamation. The controversy led to the resignations of then-BBC News CEO Deborah Turness and then-BBC Director-General Tim Davie. While Tuesday's ruling allows Trump's defamation claim to proceed, a magistrate judge previously ruled in the BBC's favor in October, ordering Trump to give a deposition by Dec. 11 unless the discovery deadline is extended beyond Dec. 18. articles.title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
articles.summary: Talks in Abu Dhabi centred around Europe's security framework, with US envoys due to meet Putin and Zelensky on Thursday.
articles.body:
Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.

Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.

Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."

"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.

Both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.

After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.

This latest round of talks had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.

For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.

For Moscow, it is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.

Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.

Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.

Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them.

Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.

Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.

There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.

Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.

Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas.

This matter was the "hardest", Kushner acknowledged, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.

"These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."

articles.title: In 1994-95, Washington crews sprayed liquid magnesium chloride on roads at three test sites before ice could build up; the treatment provided 3-10 days of ice prevention and saved $7,000 in maintenance costs
articles.summary: During a groundbreaking winter experiment, Washington crews effectively used liquid magnesium chloride to manage ice on roads, achieving up to 10 days of prevention and significant cost savings. Discover how this innovative approach is changing winter road maintenance.
articles.body: Winter road maintenance has usually meant waiting for the storm. Ice forms, crews head out with sand and chemicals and then they head out again. This experiment was conducted during the winter season between 1994 and 1995 and the Washington State Department of Transportation attempted the reverse by preparing the road so that the ice would appear on an already prepared surface. This test took place at three locations and the deicing agent used in the process was magnesium chloride in its liquid form. According to a brief provided by the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA), the outcome of the test yielded 3 to 10 days of ice management and saved $7,000 in terms of maintenance.Washington tested anti-icing at Columbia Gorge, Connell and BellinghamThe FHWA technical brief, A Preemptive Strike on Ice, describes how the Washington DOT tested anti-icing materials and methods at three locations during the winter of 1994 to 1995: Columbia Gorge, Connell and Bellingham. Cost reduction and minimising the negative impact of the application of sand and chemicals to the roadways in response to an existing storm were the goals of the department. The methodology used was taken from the Strategic Highway Research Program (SHRP). Prior to implementing the project, the maintenance staff at all sites were extensively trained in anti-icing, according to the brief by Dale Keep.Crews prepared roads with liquid magnesium chloride before ice could accumulateIn place of using sand and chemicals on roads that have heavy frost or ice, liquid magnesium chloride was used to prevent any accumulation of snow and ice on the roads. The chemical lowers the freezing point of water, which stops frost or snow from forming a strong bond with the pavement. In turn, the road remained moist or slushy, as opposed to becoming icy. Where a bond did form, crews switched to deicing to break it. According to FHWA, timing was critical, with the highway departments using weather technologies for forecasting purposes.Ice control lasted 3 to 10 days and saved $7,000 across three sitesThe period of ice prevention ranged from 3 to 10 days. The three sites sit in quite different parts of Washington, so that range reflects different conditions at each one, not a single shared result. With less labour and chemicals used, there was a saving of $7,000 and maintenance costs at all three locations, according to the above study. It was also easier and quicker to plow where necessary and there were fewer chemical applications needed, which the brief suggested was environmentally friendly. No detail of how $7,000 was shared among the three sites has been given in the brief.Federal guidance puts frost protection at 3 to 4 days on busy freewaysThe Manual Practice for an Effective Anti-Icing Program, published by FHWA in June 1996, draws on four years of anti-icing field testing by 15 State highway agencies, supported by SHRP and FHWA. According to the recommended practices section of the FHWA manual, one of the agencies in the manual sprayed a 27% magnesium chloride solution on the bridge deck in the valleys to prevent frost, at 100 L (25 gallons) per lane mile and 50 km/h (30 mph). The FHWA manual reported that a 27% magnesium chloride solution could prevent frosting on bridge decks for about a week on low-volume roads and 3 to 4 days on higher-volume freeways, depending on traffic and weather conditions.Both these periods belonged to the timeframe reported by Washington. The manual considered a liquid pre-treatment as a strategy to buy time during the first phase of a storm and stated that its effectiveness was rather short-term. The manual advises against liquid applications during freezing rain or sleet, because of the large quantity needed to keep the chemical at an effective concentration.The manual warns that anti-icing does not automatically cut costsHowever, the manual warned that anti-icing should not be considered an upgrade that would automatically bring down the cost. The manual’s post-storm assessment section says savings depend on current practice: which level of service governs, what materials are used, whether the agency does more deicing than anti-icing and which information sources it relies on. Its successful examples were equally effective maintenance, but at a reduced total cost, or greater effectiveness with the same cost. articles.title: Inside the fight against Denmark’s ‘straight up racist’ housing law
articles.summary: Residents say Denmark’s ‘ghetto law’ is breaking up strong communities, as the Supreme Court prepares to rule.
articles.body:
Copenhagen, Denmark – Under a graffiti-covered bridge in Norrebro, a multicultural, trendy district of the Danish capital, Sara touches her hijab.

“I am Muslim. The way the government and the media speak, they see me as not Western,” says the 46-year-old, who was born and raised in Denmark and asked not to use her real name.

She believes the country’s so-called “ghetto law” is a way of cracking down on Muslims, who account for little more than 4 percent of the population.

On November 23, Denmark’s Supreme Court is due to rule on a case that could shape the future of that law, which can force the sale, demolition or conversion of nonprofit homes in areas where more than half of residents are classed as “non-Western”.

In Denmark, nonprofit housing accommodates more than one million people and is open to all.

Seven families from the Nojsomhed estate in Helsingor, north of Copenhagen, are challenging their former landlord, Boliggarden, after the estate was put on the “ghetto list” in January 2020.

They argue that they were forced out because of where they or their parents come from.

In his warmly lit, cosy office space in central Copenhagen, Eddie Khawaja, the families’ lawyer, told Al Jazeera that the case boils down to whether the evaluation is “neutral” and “detached from ethnicity elements or not”.

It is the first case to reach the Supreme Court since the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) ruled last December, in cases from Mjolnerparken, an estate in Norrebro, and another estate, that the “non-Western” categorisation could amount to ethnic discrimination, and left Danish judges to decide.

Lower courts had ruled against the families, finding that “non-Western” does not describe an ethnic group.

The Supreme Court, which heard the case over two days, must now weigh that against the EU ruling.

Khawaja, who presented his closing arguments to the court on Monday, said the EU ruling opened the way for judges to look beyond the law’s wording to how politicians talked about it. In his view, “non-Western” is “a proxy for ethnic origin”.

His clients are almost all employed, well educated, and none are criminals, he said. “They are part of the community with the wrong ethnicity.”

Even if the families lose against their landlord, Khawaja said, the court must still decide whether the criterion is neutral, which could affect every estate on the lists.

The law works through lists updated by the government on December 1 every year of what were once referred to as “ghettos” but are now named “parallel societies”.

When Denmark published its first official “ghetto list” in 2010, being on it felt “stigmatising” but it did bring money for social projects, said Helle Hansen, a gregarious night-shift care worker from Gellerup in Aarhus, one of the country’s largest nonprofit housing estates.

When the annual list was published, residents of newly named estates appeared on the evening news. “We are not a ghetto,” she recalled them saying.

Under the 2018 “parallel society” law, nonprofit housing areas with at least 1,000 residents, more than half of them “non-Western”, go on the list. They must also meet two of four criteria on unemployment, crime, education and income.

After five consecutive years on the list, the areas must cut nonprofit family housing to 40 percent by 2030, through sales, demolition or conversion.

In 2021, the Social Democrat-led government removed the word “ghetto” from the law.

“Ghetto areas” became “parallel societies” and “hard ghettos” became “transformation areas”, while a new list of “prevention areas” added estates where the “non-Western” threshold is 30 percent.

An estate with the same social problems, where half or fewer residents are “non-Western”, faces no such obligation.

Khawaja said that cutting crime and raising education, incomes and employment were good aims, “but we are just saying, fine, regulate on that”.

Instead, he argued, politicians had made ethnicity “a decisive factor”.

In Gellerup, seven blocks with 408 flats were marked for demolition, said Hansen, who is part of Almen Modstand, a grassroots movement against the “ghetto law”.

Residents voted against the plan, but the wider housing association overruled them.

Under Statistics Denmark’s definition, “non-Western” covers anyone outside the EU and a short list of countries, including the United States, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

Amani Hassani, a Danish urban ethnographer and lecturer in politics and history at Brunel University London, said the criterion does something the social measures alone do not.

“What ‘non-Western’ does in Denmark is actually creating a racial category in real time,” she told Al Jazeera. “It is a question of ancestry,” she said, not citizenship.

What the category captures, she added, is “people who originate in non-white majority countries”.

Since 2020, Statistics Denmark has also published figures that separate out a third generation, which Hassani calls “descendants of descendants”.

Her grandparents came to Denmark as migrants.

“My family has been here for half a century,” she said. “The political class can speak all they want about how I am not Danish.”

Under the bridge in Copenhagen’s Norrebro district, traders work at a bustling market while students speed past on bicycles.

Sara believes religion is at the heart of the issue. “I am Muslim, and that is really what they see as non-Western,” she said.

Many people Al Jazeera spoke to said that the rhetoric used by politicians is ultimately directed at Islam.

Days after the housing law took effect, parliament adopted a resolution during a debate on the integration of Muslims, describing “parallel societies” where attempts are made to enforce Islamic customs at “the expense of Danish values”.

Ester Anker, a 27-year-old psychology student who lives in Norrebro, called the law “straight up racist” and said it was clearly aimed at Muslims. Politicians “haven’t even done a good job at hiding that fact”, she said.

Majken Felle, a 52-year-old teacher, has loved Mjolnerparken since she moved there in 2014.

For years, the list was little more than a label, she said. Then, from 2019, letters began landing in residents’ mailboxes urging them to accept “voluntary” rehousing.

Eviction notices followed, and she has since moved three times.

Yet the pressure also pulled neighbours together. Residents bound by a common cause got to know each other and met in the laundry rooms to swap what they knew about their rights, she said.

Felle speaks warmly of her former neighbours, many of them women from the Middle East who fled their countries young, raised children, and learned Danish, demonstrating, she said, resourcefulness and tenacity.

The government and housing associations underestimated many of those women, Felle said. They were supposed to just move away, but they ended up taking on the Danish state.

Hassani described the emergence of “a community of care”, where earlier arrivals help refugees navigate schools and public services.

“That’s what’s at risk. That’s what’s being dismantled here,” she said.

The estate has changed in character now, Felle said.

Most newcomers are young, mainly ethnically Danish students and expats, many from Argentina and France.

People stay for a couple of years, meaning the area has a more transitory nature. Residents do not invest in the community in the same way. Where neighbours once said hello, people now look at the ground, she said.

Mjolnerparken itself came off the list in 2023 after its population fell below 1,000, but it still has to complete its plan by the end of 2029, the housing ministry told parliament.

A four-party coalition led by Mette Frederiksen’s Social Democrats has governed Denmark since early June.

Housing is now in the hands of Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, which voted for the law in 2018.

Even a win in court may not end it, Hassani warned.

The government could use “political acrobatics”, she said, to keep targeting the same communities without the category. “They’ll just remove the label, right?” she said.

“People cannot change who they are,” she said. “And if these estates are the target today,” she asked, “who is next?”

articles.title: Kenya discharges last Ebola patient, awaits disease-free status
articles.summary: Health Minister Aden Duale says Kenya will continue to exercise prevention measures until December 23.
articles.body:
Kenya has released its last Ebola patient and begun a 42-day countdown to be declared free of the disease.

Health Minister Aden Duale made the announcement at a news conference in Nairobi on Wednesday, more than five weeks after the country recorded its first case on October 6.

Duale said Kenya would continue to exercise prevention measures until the December 23 date is reached.

The Ministry of Health previously expressed confidence that the outbreak was under control, noting that all nine confirmed cases were linked to the first patient’s contact list. This indicated that there had been no community transmission. The last case was recorded on October 19.

The first patient travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) through Uganda, and transmitted the virus to four family members and four healthcare workers.

The first patient and his mother died of Ebola, while the other seven patients fully recovered. The government identified 135 contacts who interacted with the first patient.

Elsewhere in the region, the number of infections continues to climb. In the DRC, the epicentre of the outbreak, 11,042 people have been infected and 5,387 have died, the government said on Wednesday.

The outbreak also spread to Uganda and Nigeria through individuals who travelled from the DRC.

The current Ebola outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus and has been described as one of the worst outbreaks on record.

Kenya faced travel restrictions following the Ebola outbreak, with Saudi Arabia announcing an indefinite suspension of visas on October 30. The decision affected hundreds of Kenyan workers travelling to the Gulf for employment, particularly as domestic and hotel workers.

The Ministry of Health urged Saudi Arabia to reconsider the travel restrictions, explaining that Kenya’s first Ebola case was imported and that all subsequent cases were traced to the initial patient’s contact list. The ministry said all contacts had been identified and traced in line with established outbreak-control guidelines.

Kenya tightened its border controls, designating a specific gate at the country’s main airport for passengers travelling from 10 countries that have reported Ebola cases or border those that have active cases. Passengers are being screened using thermal technology, and all new arrivals fill a health declaration form that provides their travel and health information.

Kenya will now require citizens arriving from the DRC to undergo a 21-day quarantine, Duale said.
